title: Where Your Treasure Is
subtitle: A five-session study on money, the heart, and the freedom Christ offers.
summary:
This is the small-group companion to James Bell's book Where Your Treasure Is, and it is not about the economy. It is about your heart and what it has quietly done with money. It walks slowly through five sessions on the heart that follows its treasure, the contentment we keep mistaking for resignation, the rich fool who confused a full barn with a safe soul, the anxiety that drives our reaching, and the strange freedom of the open hand. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters the generous and indicts the greedy, because Bell does not believe the line runs there. It catches the man who gives and still grips, the woman who has little and still worships what she lacks, the giver who has used his giving to stop the question before it reached his heart. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has lain awake doing arithmetic he called prudence. He has felt his chest loosen at a number in an account and called the loosening peace. He has loved his five sons and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough. He writes from inside the indictment about money, not above it. So will you. The question is never whether you may have money. The question is what your heart has done with it, and whether you can hear, under all the wanting, the voice of the One who became poor so that you could be free.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Where Your Treasure Is
sessions.aim: To see that the heart does not lead the treasure but follows it, and to stop asking whether money is allowed and start asking where our treasure has already taught our heart to live.
sessions.summary: We assume the heart chooses first and the wallet obeys, that we love a thing and then spend on it. Jesus reverses the order. Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The treasure goes first and the heart follows it like a dog on a leash, which means the surest way to find what you actually love is not to ask but to look at where the money and the worry already go. Bell builds the session on Matthew 6, on the moth and the rust and the thief, on the eye that is the lamp of the body, on the impossibility of two masters. He takes seriously the reader who hears all this as guilt about money and answers him with the text. The warning is not against having treasure. It is against laying it up where it cannot survive, where the moth gets in and the heart goes with it. Then the verdict Jesus will not soften. You cannot serve God and money. Not should not. Cannot. The session is not about your budget. It is about the leash, and where it has already pulled your heart while you were not watching.

keyScripture.why: Jesus reverses the order we assume, saying that where the treasure is the heart will follow, so that our spending and our worry are not the result of our loves but the map of them.

discussion.q: Jesus says where your treasure is, there your heart will be also, putting the treasure first and the heart second. Before tonight, did you assume your heart leads your money, or your money leads your heart?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before defining anything. Most people in the pew assume the heart leads, that they love God and merely spend on lesser things, that the wallet is downstream of devotion. Jesus reverses it. The point is not to win the argument tonight but to let the room feel the unsettling order Jesus actually states, that the treasure trains the heart and not the other way around. Land it on honesty.

discussion.q: Jesus says the way to find your heart is to look at your treasure. If a stranger studied only your spending and your worry for a month, what would he conclude you love most, and would he be wrong?
discussion.behind: Push past the abstract into evidence. People will defend their stated loves, but the question asks for the visible trail, the money and the lying-awake. Bell's point is that the worry is as revealing as the spending. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone. You want each person, including the leader, to read his own ledger honestly and notice the gap between what he says he treasures and where the leash actually pulls.

discussion.q: Bell takes seriously the person who hears all this as shame about money, and answers that Jesus does not forbid treasure but warns where we lay it up. What is true in the worry that this teaching is just guilt, and what does the text actually say?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness early. Jesus says lay up treasure, only somewhere the moth and rust and thief cannot reach. The warning is not against having but against storing it where it will rot and take the heart down with it. Make sure no one leaves thinking the answer is to despise provision or feel guilty for owning. The error is the location, not the having.

discussion.q: Jesus says no one can serve two masters, that you will love one and despise the other. Where in an ordinary week do you feel the two masters pulling, and which one usually wins without your noticing?
discussion.behind: Make the abstraction concrete. The two masters rarely announce a contest. Money wins quietly, in the decision made on autopilot, the calendar arranged around earning, the rest given to the second master while the first gets the leftover minutes. Help the room locate the moment of divided service, the place the leash tightens and they follow without a thought.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has loved his sons and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough, that the leash has pulled his own heart while he watched. Where has your treasure pulled your heart somewhere you did not mean to go?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. You are not hunting for shame. You want each person, including you the leader, inside the indictment, because the gospel of the open hand means nothing until you have felt the leash on your own neck. Go first if the room is slow. Name a real place your treasure has trained your heart, and the room will follow you into honesty.

objections.objection: This is just shame about money dressed up as theology. Jesus is not against owning things or saving for the future. He had a treasurer, ate at rich men's tables, and never told most people he met to get rid of their possessions.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Jesus does not forbid treasure. He says lay it up, only somewhere it cannot rot, where the moth and rust and thief cannot reach it. Provision is not the sin. The Bible honors the ant who stores in summer. Then make the distinction gently. The warning is about location and about leash. Where you put the treasure is where the heart goes, and a heart laid up where moths eat is a heart you will lose without ever deciding to. The question is never whether you may have money. It is whether your money has quietly come to have you.

objections.objection: I do not even think about money that much, so this whole study is for greedy people, not me. I live simply and do not chase wealth.
objections.response: Take the claim seriously, because simplicity is a real good and Bell will not sneer at it. But notice what the not-thinking can hide. The two masters do not fight loudly in the man who has made peace with one of them. Jesus warns the person who does not chase wealth as much as the one who does, because the heart can serve money through fear of not having it as easily as through hunger to get more. The anxious frugal man and the reaching ambitious man may be bowing to the same master in different postures. Do not assume that because you are not greedy you are free. Look at your worry, not only your wanting.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you traced the leash from your heart to your treasure, where would it actually lead, and is that where you meant your heart to live?
sessions.practice: This week, keep a quiet record for three days of where your money goes and, harder, where your worry goes. Do not change anything yet. At the end, read the two lists as a map of what you love, and write down the one place the map surprised you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, You said our hearts would follow our treasure, and we have spent years pretending it was the other way around. Show us where we have laid it up, where the moth is already at work, where our hearts have wandered after it without our permission. We cannot serve You and money both, and we have tried, and we are tired. Loosen the leash. Teach us to lay up our treasure where You are, so that our hearts can finally come home to You. In the name of Jesus, who is the treasure that does not rot. Amen.
reflection: If my treasure trains my heart and not the other way around, what has my treasure been quietly teaching my heart to love?
Where have I laid up treasure in a place the moth can reach, and what part of my heart have I lost there without noticing?
When I imagine serving God with my money the way I serve money with my attention, what rises up in me to resist it?
sessions.teaching:
We carry an assumption so deep we never examine it, that the heart leads and the wallet follows. We believe we love a thing first and spend on it second, that devotion comes before the dollar. Jesus says the opposite, and the reversal should stop us cold. Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. And then the hinge. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. He puts the treasure first. The heart follows it like a dog on a leash, going where it is pulled, and the surest way to find what you actually love is not to search your feelings but to follow your money and your worry, because they have already gone ahead of your heart to the place it will arrive.

Take the reader who hears all of this as guilt about money, and take him seriously, because Bell has been him. He says Jesus must be against owning, against saving, against the simple human work of providing for those you love. But read what Jesus actually says. He does not say do not lay up treasure. He says do not lay it up here, where the moth and the rust and the thief can reach it, where everything you store is already dissolving while you stack it. The command is not to stop treasuring. It is to treasure somewhere the loss cannot follow. The sin is not the having. The sin is the location, and the location is fatal, because where the treasure is the heart will be, and a heart stored where moths eat is a heart you will lose without ever choosing to lose it.

Then Jesus says a strange thing about the eye. The eye is the lamp of the body, and if your eye is healthy your whole body is full of light, but if your eye is bad your whole body is full of darkness. The eye is what you fix your gaze on, what you keep looking toward, and the word he uses for a bad eye is the word for a greedy, grasping eye, the eye that is always doing arithmetic on what it sees. A grasping eye darkens the whole body. You think you are simply being careful, simply keeping an eye on the numbers, and the keeping of the eye on the numbers is itself the darkness spreading into everything you are. And here I have to stand inside it, because I have a grasping eye and I have called it stewardship. I have lain awake running the figures and called the lying awake prudence. I have loved my sons and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough, and the reaching darkened the very love it claimed to serve.

Now the verdict Jesus will not let us soften. No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money. He does not say you should not. He says you cannot, because the heart will not run two ultimate currents at once. It is not a rule. It is a description of how a heart is wired. And the cruelty of mammon as a master is that it never demands the contest out loud. It does not ask you to renounce God. It only asks for your trust, a little more each year, until you discover that the second master has been getting your mornings and your worry and your best attention while the first master got whatever was left.

This is law before grace, and the law has named me. My eye is bad. My treasure is laid up in the wrong place and my heart has followed it there. But the gospel under this is the only thing that loosens the leash, because the One who said your heart will follow your treasure went and became our treasure, the pearl of great price, the field with the gift hidden in it, and then made himself poor to the point of a borrowed grave so that we could store our hearts in him where no moth has ever been. You do not loosen your grip on money in order to earn him. You loosen it because he has already become the treasure that cannot be stolen, and a heart laid up there is finally, for the first time, safe.

scriptureStudy.note: Do not lay up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy. Notice he does not say do not lay up treasure at all. He names the place and the problem with the place, that everything stored here is dissolving even as you stack it.

Lay up treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys. The command is still to treasure. The only change is the address. Jesus is not against the storing. He is against storing your heart somewhere it will rot.

For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The treasure leads and the heart follows. This single sentence overturns how we think we work, and it makes our bank statement a more honest confession than our prayers.
The eye is the lamp of the body. What you fix your gaze on fills the whole of you with light or with dark. The eye is not neutral. It pours what it watches through the entire body.

If your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. The word for bad eye is the grasping, greedy eye. A heart always calculating its gain is not merely distracted. It is darkening, all the way through.
No one can serve two masters. You cannot serve God and money. Not should not, cannot. The heart will not run two ultimate currents, and mammon is the master that never asks for the contest out loud.

Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Luke sets the same verdict after a command to sell and give, sharpening it. The treasure that has already gone ahead to heaven is the only treasure your heart can safely follow.

The treasure hidden in a field, the pearl of great price. The man sells all he has, not as loss but as the gladdest trade ever made, because he has found the one treasure worth the leash of his whole heart.

sessions.title: The Secret of Contentment
sessions.aim: To recover contentment as a learned freedom and not a resignation, and to expose the lie that has us forever one purchase away from a peace that keeps moving.
sessions.summary: Paul writes from a prison cell that he has learned the secret of being content in any circumstance, full or hungry, plenty or want. The word learned should stop us, because we treat contentment as a temperament some people are born with and others are not. Paul says it is a secret, a thing learned, and he learned it in places we would call ruin. The session takes the strong case of the reader who hears contentment as a counsel to settle, to stop striving, to accept less than you deserve, and answers it from the text. Paul is not resigned. He is free, and the freedom runs in both directions, knowing how to abound and how to be brought low, neither the abundance nor the lack able to move him off his center. Then the verdict that cannot be improved. Godliness with contentment is great gain. The love of money is not cured by getting more money, because the wanting is a thirst that drinking salt water deepens. Contentment is not the death of desire. It is desire finally aimed at the one thing that satisfies it. The session is about the lie that keeps the peace always one purchase ahead, and the secret Paul learned that finally stopped the chase.

keyScripture.why: Paul says he learned to be content in any circumstance, naming contentment as a learned secret and not a temperament, and a freedom that abundance and want are equally unable to disturb.

discussion.q: Paul says he learned to be content, that it was a secret he had to be taught. Most of us treat contentment as a personality some people get and others do not. What changes when you hear it is learned, and learned in a prison?
discussion.behind: Open on the word learned, because it dismantles the excuse. If contentment is temperament, you are off the hook, you simply were not built for it. Paul says it is a secret learned in want, which means it is available to you and also that it will cost you the schooling. Land the room on the hope and the cost together, that you can have it but you will be taught it, usually in places you would not choose.

discussion.q: We live as if peace is one purchase away, one raise, one paid-off debt, one more thing, and then the line keeps moving the moment we reach it. Where has the line moved on you, and did you notice it move?
discussion.behind: Surface the chase honestly. Everyone has reached a number or a thing they once believed would be enough, and found the enough had quietly relocated. The aim is recognition, not despair. Help the room feel the pattern, that the satisfaction never arrives because the wanting itself manufactures the next horizon. The man who drinks salt water to quench his thirst is not failing to drink enough.

discussion.q: Bell says contentment is not the death of desire but desire finally aimed at the thing that can satisfy it. How is that different from the resignation we usually mean when we tell someone to just be content?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. People hear contentment as settling, as killing your wanting, as accepting less. Paul is not resigned, he is free, and free in both directions. The point is that contentment redirects desire rather than extinguishing it. Do not let the room conclude the goal is to want nothing. The goal is to want the right thing so deeply the lesser wants lose their grip.

discussion.q: Paul says he learned both how to be brought low and how to abound, as if abundance were as dangerous to contentment as lack. Why might having plenty be just as much a threat to a contented heart as not having enough?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. We assume only scarcity threatens peace, but Paul names abundance as something he had to learn to survive. Plenty breeds the quiet assumption that you are secure, that you have arranged your own safety, and that assumption is its own kind of poverty. Make sure the comfortable in the room feel the warning aimed at them and not only at the struggling.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has felt his chest loosen at a number in an account and called the loosening peace, mistaking arithmetic for contentment. Where have you mistaken a secured circumstance for the peace only Christ gives?
discussion.behind: Close on self-implication. The counterfeit of contentment is circumstance arranged in your favor, the loosening you feel when the numbers are good, which evaporates the moment they turn. Invite people to name the place they have called a feeling peace that was really just a comfortable circumstance. Go first. Name the number that has loosened your own chest and lied to you about your soul.

objections.objection: Telling people to be content is just a way to keep them passive and accepting of less than they deserve. It is a sedative, a way to make the struggling settle and stop wanting better for themselves.
objections.response: Hear the worry, because contentment has been misused exactly this way, preached at people to keep them quiet. But that is not what Paul means, and the text proves it. Paul is not passive. He works, he travels, he labors harder than anyone, he is anything but settled. His contentment is not the absence of effort but the absence of dependence, a freedom that lets him strive without being enslaved to the outcome. He has learned how to abound and how to be brought low, which is not resignation but mastery. The contented person is not the one who has stopped wanting better. He is the one whose peace no longer hangs on whether better arrives.

objections.objection: It is easy to talk about contentment when your needs are met, but you cannot tell a person who genuinely lacks to simply be content. Real need is real, and spiritualizing it is cruel.
objections.response: Grant this fully, because it is true and the study must never shame the person in real want. Need is real, and Scripture takes it seriously enough to command provision for it. But notice who is speaking. Paul writes about contentment in hunger from inside hunger, in want from inside want, in a cell from inside a cell. He has not theorized contentment from comfort. He has learned it from the bottom, which is the only place it can be honestly learned and the only place it has any authority to be spoken. He is not telling the hungry to feel fine about hunger. He is telling them there is a peace hunger cannot reach, and he knows because hunger could not reach his.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the one thing you still secretly believe would finally make you content, and how many times has something like it already failed to?
sessions.practice: This week, name out loud, to God and to one trusted person, the specific thing you have been treating as your missing piece, the purchase or raise or change you believe would settle you. Then sit with the question of what you would still lack if you got it, and write down what you hear.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have chased a peace that keeps moving, always one thing ahead of us, and we have called the chase ambition and the exhaustion realism. We did not know contentment was something we could learn, and we are afraid of the schooling. Teach us anyway. Teach us in plenty not to trust the plenty, and in want not to be ruled by the want. Aim our desire at You, who alone can satisfy it, until the line stops moving because we have finally arrived at the only enough there is. Through Christ, who learned obedience in a harder school than ours. Amen.
reflection: If contentment is learned and not given, what is the school God has put me in, and have I been refusing the lesson?
What number, purchase, or change have I been treating as the thing that will finally settle me, and why do I still believe it after everything that has not?
Where have I felt the loosening of a secured circumstance and called it peace, and what happened to that peace when the circumstance turned?
sessions.teaching:
Paul writes a sentence from a prison cell that should be impossible to write from a prison cell. I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content. The word that should arrest us is learned. We do not talk about contentment as something learned. We talk about it as a temperament, a disposition, a gift some people received in the cradle and others did not, so that the discontented are simply unlucky in their wiring. Paul calls it a secret, a thing into which he was initiated, a skill acquired the way any hard skill is acquired, through repetition in conditions he would not have chosen. I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. The freedom was not native to him. He was schooled in it, and the schoolroom was want.

Take the reader who hears the word contentment and bristles, because contentment has been weaponized, preached at struggling people as a way to keep them quiet and accepting of less than they should have. He says this teaching is a sedative. Hear him, because he is half right about how the word has been abused. But look at the man saying it. Paul is the least passive person in the New Testament. He works with his hands, crosses seas, plants churches, argues, suffers, drives himself past the limits of his body. His contentment is not the absence of striving. It is the absence of dependence. He strives like a man who has nothing riding on the outcome, because his peace is not stored in the outcome. That is not resignation. That is the rarest freedom there is, and it runs in both directions, knowing how to be brought low and knowing how to abound, as if the abundance were as dangerous as the lack.

And it is. We assume only scarcity threatens peace. Paul names plenty as something he had to learn to survive, because abundance whispers that you have secured yourself, that the danger is handled, that you can finally rest in what you have arranged. It is a lie, and it is a more comfortable lie than poverty's, which is exactly why it is harder to detect. The poor man knows he is not safe. The rich man has been told he is, by the very thing that cannot keep him. I know this from the inside. I have felt my chest loosen at a number in an account and called the loosening peace. It was not peace. It was a circumstance, and circumstances turn, and the peace turned with it, which is how I learned it had never been peace at all.

Here is why the chase never ends. Paul tells Timothy that godliness with contentment is great gain, and then names the disease underneath our discontent, that those who desire to be rich fall into a snare, because the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. The love of money is not cured by acquiring money. The wanting is a thirst that the drinking deepens, the way salt water deepens thirst. Every purchase that promised to be enough relocates the enough one step further out, and we mistake the moving line for a sign that we simply have not reached it yet. We have not failed to drink enough. We are drinking the wrong water.

So contentment is not the death of desire, which is what we fear it is. It is desire finally aimed at the one thing built to satisfy it. The discontented heart is not wanting too much. It is wanting too small, pouring an infinite longing into finite things that crack under the weight every time. And the gospel under this is the only thing that can redirect the thirst, because the secret Paul learned has a name. I can do all things through him who strengthens me. The contentment was never self-generated calm. It was a Person, present in the cell, more real to him than the chains, the treasure that does not move when the circumstances move. You will not argue yourself content. You will not acquire yourself content. You will be brought, slowly and usually through loss, to the only well that does not run dry, and there, with your thirst finally drinking the right water, the line will stop moving, because for the first time in your life you will have arrived.

scriptureStudy.note: I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content. The verb is learned. Contentment is not a temperament you were born with or without. It is a secret you are taught, which means it is available to you and will cost you the schooling.

I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. The freedom runs both ways. Abundance is named as a thing he had to learn to survive, as dangerous to a settled heart as lack, because plenty lies about your safety.

I can do all things through him who strengthens me. The famous verse is the secret of contentment, not a promise of success. The strength is not to achieve anything but to be content in everything, full or hungry.

Godliness with contentment is great gain. Paul sets contentment beside godliness and calls the pair the real wealth, the gain the chase keeps promising and never delivers, because the chase is the disease and contentment the cure.

If we have food and clothing, with these we will be content. The bar is startlingly low, food and covering, the bare provision of a life. Everything above it is gift, not entitlement, and the heart that grasps it as owed has already lost contentment.

Those who desire to be rich fall into a snare. The verb is desire, not possess. The trap is the wanting, the reaching, which is why getting more never springs it, because acquiring feeds the very craving it promised to satisfy.

Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, I will never leave you. Contentment is grounded not in having enough but in having a Presence that does not leave when the having does.

The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. The not wanting is not the absence of need but the presence of the Shepherd. The well is a Person, and the heart that drinks there finally stops thirsting after the wrong water.

memoryVerse.text: But godliness with contentment is great gain.

sessions.title: The Rich Fool and the Soul You Forgot
sessions.aim: To hear Jesus call a successful man a fool, and to face the question the full barn was built to keep us from asking, whose will these things be when your soul is required of you.
sessions.summary: A man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute, and Jesus refuses the role of judge and tells a story instead, about a man whose land produced so well he had to tear down his barns and build bigger ones. The man does everything right by every standard we admire. He plans, he saves, he secures the future, he tells his soul to rest. And God calls him a fool, not for a crime but for a blindness, for building a future for a body while forgetting he had a soul, for storing up treasure for himself and not being rich toward God. The session takes the reader who finds this unfair, who sees a prudent man punished for ordinary success, and answers from the text. The fool's error is not the barn. It is the word my, repeated until there is no room in his speech for anyone but himself, and the word soul, used to mean nothing more than appetite. Then the verdict. This night your soul is required of you, and the things you prepared, whose will they be. Bell stands inside it, having built barns he called prudence while his soul went unaddressed. The session is about the soul the full barn lets us forget.

keyScripture.why: God names a successful, prudent man a fool and reveals that his soul is required this very night, exposing the blindness of a life that secured everything except the one thing that could be lost forever.

discussion.q: A man asks Jesus to make his brother divide the inheritance, a fair request, and Jesus refuses and warns instead about covetousness. Why do you think Jesus would not even step into a money dispute, and what was he refusing to become?
discussion.behind: Open on the refusal. The man wants Jesus as an arbiter, a fixer of his financial grievance, and Jesus will not be reduced to that, because he sees the covetousness under the fairness. The point is to notice how money disputes present themselves as justice while masking a deeper grip. Help the room feel that Jesus is after the heart under the request, not the merits of the case.

discussion.q: The rich fool does everything we would praise. He plans, saves, secures the future, and tells himself to rest. Which of his actions, on its own, would you call wrong, and if none, then what exactly does God call foolish?
discussion.behind: Force the difficulty. None of the man's individual acts are crimes. He is prudent by every standard we teach our children. The aim is to make the room sit in the discomfort that God calls him a fool anyway, so they cannot locate the sin in any single behavior and must find it where Jesus puts it, in the orientation of the whole, the self at the center and the soul forgotten.

discussion.q: In his short speech the man says my crops, my barns, my grain, my goods, my soul, the word my over and over, and uses soul to mean nothing but appetite. What does his vocabulary reveal that his behavior alone would not?
discussion.behind: Get into the language, because Jesus put it there on purpose. The man cannot speak a sentence without himself at the center, no neighbor, no God, no one in need. And he tells his soul to eat and drink, reducing the soul to a stomach. The point is that the grip shows up in the grammar. Invite people to hear their own inner monologue about money and notice how crowded it is with my and how thin its idea of the soul.

discussion.q: Bell says the barn is not the sin, that the error is a man building a magnificent future for a body while forgetting he had a soul. Where have you built carefully for your future and left your soul entirely unaddressed?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the session. We plan for retirement, for the kids' college, for the emergency, and almost never plan for the soul that will outlast all of it. The aim is honest recognition, not guilt about saving. Press on the imbalance, the elaborate provision for the body and the neglected provision for the soul, and let the room feel the foolishness of securing everything that can be lost and nothing that cannot.

discussion.q: God asks, this night your soul is required of you, and the things you prepared, whose will they be. If tonight were that night, what have you spent your life preparing, and who would it go to, and what would you wish you had done instead?
discussion.behind: Close on the verdict and the self-implication. The question is not morbid, it is clarifying, the thing the full barn was built to keep us from asking. Bell admits he has built barns he called prudence while his soul went unaddressed. Invite people to let the question do its work without rushing past it. Go first. Sit in the silence. The arithmetic people do here is the point.

objections.objection: This is unfair. The man did nothing wrong. He worked hard, his land prospered, he planned responsibly, and Jesus punishes him for the crime of being successful and prudent. Are we not supposed to save and plan?
objections.response: Grant the force of it, because the man breaks no commandment, and Scripture does commend saving and planning. The fool is not condemned for the barn. Read his speech and you find the sin Jesus is naming. He says my crops, my barns, my goods, my soul, and in the whole monologue there is no God, no neighbor, no one but himself, and he tells his soul to eat and be merry, as though a soul were a stomach. The folly is not the planning. It is a man who secured everything that could be taken from him and ignored the one thing that could be lost forever, who built for a body and forgot he had a soul. Plan for your future. Just do not forget which future is longer.

objections.objection: Stories about death and judgment are just fear tactics to make people give away their money or stop enjoying what they have earned. Why can a person not simply enjoy the fruit of his labor in peace?
objections.response: Sit with the part that is true, because Scripture does say there is good in enjoying the fruit of your labor, and the study will not make a sin of a good meal. But the parable is not a fear tactic, it is a fact placed where we keep it hidden. The man was not threatened into anything. He simply did not know it was his last night, which none of us know about ours, and the parable does the kindness of saying so out loud. Far from forbidding enjoyment, it asks why we postpone the only enjoyment that lasts, telling our souls to rest in a security the soul was never built to find in a barn. The point is not to fear death. It is to stop pretending we have more time than we do to become rich toward God.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your soul were required of you tonight, what have you spent your years preparing, and would you call it wise?
sessions.practice: This week, write two short lists side by side, what you have done in the last year to secure your body and its future, and what you have done in the same year to become rich toward God. Do not perform either list. Just set them next to each other, and write down what the comparison shows you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have built our barns with great care and let our souls go unaddressed, and we did not even notice the imbalance, because everyone around us was doing the same. We have said my so many times we forgot the things were ever a gift. Forgive us. Remind us that this night, any night, our souls could be required, and the barns will go to someone else. Make us rich toward You, where the wealth cannot be inherited away or lost in a turn of the market, where the soul we forgot is finally fed. Through Christ, who emptied His own barns for us. Amen.
reflection: If God called this prudent man a fool, on what grounds, and would the same grounds reach me?
How elaborately have I provided for my body and its future, and how little, by comparison, have I provided for my soul?
When I imagine my soul required of me tonight, what does the imagining tell me I have been treating as more permanent than it is?
sessions.teaching:
A man interrupts Jesus mid-teaching with a financial grievance. Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. It is not an unreasonable request. He has been wronged, or believes he has, and he wants the famous rabbi to settle it in his favor. Jesus refuses. Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you. And then he says the thing the man did not ask about and needed to hear. Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions. He will not be reduced to a referee in a money dispute, because he can see what the man cannot, that under the language of fairness is a grip, and the grip is the real problem, not the inheritance.

Then he tells a story, and the story is about a man we would admire. The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, what shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops. I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods, and I will say to my soul, soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years, relax, eat, drink, be merry. Read it as the man's neighbors would have read it. Here is a success story. Here is a man whose hard work paid off, who planned ahead, who secured his future, who earned the right to rest. There is not a single illegal or even unkind act in the whole account. By every standard we hand our children, he did it right.

And God said to him, fool. Not thief. Not oppressor. Fool. This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be. Take the reader who finds this unfair, who sees a prudent man struck down for ordinary success, and take him seriously, because the parable is genuinely shocking if you think the sin is the barn. But the sin is not the barn. Listen to the man speak, because Jesus wrote his speech with terrible care. My crops. My barns. My grain. My goods. My soul. In the whole of his interior monologue there is no God, no neighbor, no poor man at the gate, no one but himself, the word my falling again and again until it has crowded everyone else out of his world. And then the worst word. He says to his soul, relax, eat, drink. He has a soul, and the only thing he can think to do with it is feed it like a stomach. He has reduced the deepest thing in him to an appetite.

That is the folly. Not that he stored grain, but that he built a magnificent future for a body and forgot entirely that he had a soul. He secured everything that could be taken from him and ignored the one thing that could be lost forever. And I have to say it before I say it of anyone else, because I have built barns I called prudence while my soul went years without being addressed. I have planned for the body's future in detail and left the soul's future to chance, as if the shorter life were the one that needed the planning. The rich fool is not a stranger I get to judge from a distance. He is the man I become every time I confuse securing my circumstances with tending my soul.

Then the verdict, and Jesus will not soften it. This night your soul is required of you. The man thought he had years. He had hours. And the things he prepared, whose will they be, because they will not be his, they were never finally his, they will pass to someone who did not earn them while the soul he neglected goes to meet a God he never once mentioned. So is the one, Jesus says, who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. There is the contrast that saves the parable from being mere terror. Rich toward God. There is another kind of wealth, stored in another place, that the night cannot require away. The gospel under this is that the One telling the story emptied His own barns entirely, owned nothing at the end but the clothes they gambled for, and made Himself poor precisely so that fools like us, caught securing the wrong future, could be made rich toward God in the only account that survives the night.

scriptureStudy.note: Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. The man wants Jesus as an arbiter of his grievance. The request sounds like justice, but Jesus hears the grip underneath and will not be reduced to a referee over it.

Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. The warning is be on guard, because this is the idol that does not announce itself, hiding inside ordinary planning.

What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops. The crisis is a surplus, a good problem, the kind we would envy. The parable begins not with a sin but with success, which is what makes its verdict so unsettling.

I will tear down my barns and build larger ones. Notice there is no other plan, no thought of the neighbor or the poor, only a bigger container for himself. The bigger barn is the only imagination a self-centered abundance can produce.

Soul, you have ample goods, relax, eat, drink, be merry. He speaks to his soul and offers it food and ease, reducing the deepest thing in him to a stomach. The tragedy is not greed but a soul addressed as if it were an appetite.

Fool, this night your soul is required of you. God names the prudent man a fool, and the things he prepared pass to another. He secured all that could be taken and forgot the one thing that could be lost forever.

So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. The contrast saves the parable. There is another wealth, rich toward God, that the night cannot require away, and it is the only kind worth a life.

I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool. The Preacher names the same horror, the things you prepared passing to someone who did not earn them, vanity under the sun.
