sessions.title: Do Not Be Anxious: Money and the Worried Heart
sessions.aim: To name money-anxiety as a disorder of trust rather than a personality trait, and to hear Jesus address the worried heart not with a budget but with a Father.
sessions.summary: Right after Jesus says you cannot serve God and money, he says therefore do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or wear. The therefore matters. Anxiety about provision is not a separate topic from the love of money. It is the same idol felt from the underside, the worship of money turned inside out into fear of not having it. The session walks through the birds who do not store and the lilies who do not toil, and it takes the reader who hears do not worry as an impossible or even insulting command, the kind of thing said by people who have never lain awake over a bill, and answers it from the text. Jesus does not shame the worried. He reasons with them, gently, about a Father who feeds the birds and clothes the grass and knows what they need before they ask. The command is not stop feeling, it is look up, consider, remember whose child you are. Then the verdict that reorders everything. Seek first the kingdom, and all these things will be added to you. Bell stands inside it, a man who has lain awake doing arithmetic and calling the lying awake responsibility. The session is about the worried heart and the Father it keeps forgetting it has.

keyScripture.why: Jesus addresses the anxious heart not with a financial plan but with a Father who feeds the birds, naming worry about provision as a failure of trust that the love and care of God is meant to heal.

discussion.q: Jesus says you cannot serve God and money, and then immediately, therefore do not be anxious about your life. Why do you think he connects the love of money and anxiety about money, and how are they the same thing felt differently?
discussion.behind: Open on the therefore, because it is the key that most people miss. We treat greed and worry as opposite problems, the greedy want more and the anxious just want enough. Jesus treats them as one idol from two sides, the same trust misplaced, surfacing as hunger in one heart and fear in another. Help the room see that the worried person is not exempt from the money idol but is bowing to it in a different posture.

discussion.q: Jesus points to the birds, who neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet are fed. He is not telling us to stop working. What is he actually asking us to notice about who does the feeding?
discussion.behind: Get the point of the birds right, because it is easy to misread as a command to be irresponsible. The birds work hard, they forage all day, but they do not store and they do not control the outcome, and they are fed anyway by a Father. The aim is to move the room's eyes off their own provision and onto the Provider, to feel the difference between working and trusting the work to save you.

discussion.q: Bell says worry is the love of money felt from the underside, the worship of money wearing the face of the fear of not having it. Does that reframe land for you, or do you want to defend your worry as just being responsible?
discussion.behind: Let people push back honestly, because many will feel their anxiety is realism, not idolatry. There is a real distinction between planning and worrying, and the room should find it. But the reframe is meant to expose the worry that has crossed from prudent planning into a fear that rules the heart, the lying awake that no amount of planning quiets. Keep the distinction between honest care and idolatrous fear clear and let each person locate the line in himself.

discussion.q: Jesus does not shame the worried. He reasons gently, consider the birds, look at the lilies, your Father knows what you need. Why does he answer anxiety with a Father instead of a budget, and what does that tell you about what anxiety actually is?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The cure Jesus offers is not better financial management but a restored relationship, because the disease is not a planning failure but a trust failure, a forgetting of whose child you are. Help the room feel that you cannot reason yourself out of money-anxiety by improving your spreadsheet, because the wound is relational, and only the knowledge of a Father who knows and provides reaches it.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has lain awake doing arithmetic and called the lying awake responsibility. Where have you dressed your anxiety as virtue, calling it being careful or being a good provider, when underneath it was fear that God would not come through?
discussion.behind: Close on self-implication. The most defended form of money-anxiety wears the costume of responsibility, so that to question it feels like questioning love for one's family. Invite gentle recognition that the sleepless arithmetic is often not prudence but a fear that the Father will not provide. Go first. Name your own three-in-the-morning math and what it has revealed about how little you trust the One who feeds the birds.

objections.objection: Telling an anxious person do not worry is useless and a little cruel. It is the sort of thing said by people who have never missed a payment or lain awake wondering how to feed their kids. You cannot command a feeling away.
objections.response: Hear the protest fully, because a glib do not worry has wounded a lot of people, and the study must never hand it out cheaply. But look at how Jesus actually gives the command. He does not bark it and move on. He reasons, patiently, consider the birds, look at the lilies, your heavenly Father knows what you need, building a case for trust rather than demanding a feeling. He is not commanding you to stop feeling by willpower. He is giving the heart something true to rest on so the feeling has somewhere else to go. And he says it as one acquainted with grief and hunger, not from a comfortable distance. This is not a slogan. It is a Father reasoning with a frightened child.

objections.objection: If I do not worry about money, who will? Worry is what makes me responsible, what makes me plan and save and provide for my family. Take away my anxiety and I will be reckless.
objections.response: Notice the assumption hiding in this, that worry is the engine of responsibility, that without fear you would not provide. The birds work hard and do not worry, which means anxiety and diligence are not the same thing, and you can lose the one without losing the other. Worry has never once added a dollar to an account or an hour to a life. It is not the fuel of provision, it is the tax on it, draining the very person who is trying to provide. Jesus does not tell you to stop planning. He tells you to stop carrying the outcome as though it rested on you, because it rests on a Father, and the planning will go better, not worse, once the fear is no longer driving it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the financial fear you carry to bed with you, and what does carrying it say about who you believe is finally responsible for your life?
sessions.practice: This week, when the money-worry rises, especially at night, do not try to argue it down. Instead, say out loud one true thing Jesus gave the anxious, that the Father feeds the birds and knows what you need, and write down afterward whether naming the Father did anything the arithmetic never could.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, You feed the birds that do not store and clothe the grass that is here today and gone tomorrow, and still we lie awake as if You did not know we were here. We have called our fear responsibility and our sleepless arithmetic love, and underneath it was a child who does not believe his Father will come through. Forgive us. Quiet the math. Remind us that You know what we need before we ask, and teach us to seek first Your kingdom, trusting You with the rest the way the birds do, who have never once been disappointed in You. Through Christ, who had nowhere to lay His head and was never once forsaken. Amen.
reflection: Where has my anxiety about money crossed the line from honest planning into a fear that rules me, and how would I know the difference if I looked?
If worry is the love of money felt from the underside, what does my particular worry reveal about what I am really trusting to keep me safe?
What would change in how I sleep, plan, and give if I actually believed my Father knows what I need before I ask Him?
sessions.teaching:
Watch where Jesus puts the command, because the placement is the argument. He has just said no one can serve two masters, that you cannot serve God and money. And then, without a paragraph break, therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. That therefore is doing enormous work. Jesus is saying that anxiety about provision is not a separate subject from the love of money. It is the same idol, felt from the underside. The greedy man worships money by reaching for more of it. The anxious man worships money by being terrified of not having enough of it. They look like opposite problems, the hunger and the fear, but they are the same misplaced trust wearing two different faces, and Jesus treats them as one disease because they are.

Then he reasons with us, and the gentleness of how he reasons matters as much as what he says. Look at the birds of the air, they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they. Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow, they neither toil nor spin, yet Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. He is not telling us to stop working. The birds work hard, they forage from dawn, they are not idle. What the birds do not do is store against tomorrow as though the storing were what kept them alive, and what they do not do is carry the outcome, because the outcome is carried by a Father. Jesus is moving our eyes off our own provision and onto the Provider, off the barn and onto the One who fills it.

Take the reader who hears do not be anxious and feels insulted, because that is a fair thing to feel if you have ever lain awake over a bill. He says this is a command for people who have never been afraid, the sort of thing said by those who have never missed a payment. Take him seriously, because a glib do not worry, tossed at a frightened person, is a small cruelty, and the church has done it. But look again at how Jesus says it. He does not command the feeling away and walk off. He builds a case, patiently, consider, look, are you not of more value, your Father knows what you need before you ask him. He is not demanding that the frightened child stop being frightened by sheer willpower. He is giving the child something true and solid to rest on, a Father who sees and knows and feeds, so that the fear finally has somewhere else to go. And he says it as a man who would die with nothing, who knew hunger, not from the comfortable distance the objection imagines.

And I have to climb down into this one, because money-anxiety is my native tongue. I have lain awake at three in the morning doing arithmetic, running the numbers against the bills against the future, and I have called the lying awake responsibility. I have called it being a good provider, being careful, looking after my five sons, and all of that language was a costume over a simpler thing, a fear that the Father would not come through, that it was finally up to me, that if I stopped worrying the bottom would fall out. The worry felt like love. It was actually a quiet accusation against God, a refusal to believe He knew I was here. And the worst of it is that the worry never once helped, never added a dollar or an hour, only taxed the very strength I needed for the day in front of me.

Then the verdict that reorders the whole anxious life. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. He does not say stop caring about food and clothing. He says stop putting them first, stop building your life around securing them, because that order is exactly backward and it is eating you alive. Put the kingdom first, the Father first, and the provision falls into its proper place behind Him, added rather than chased. The cure for money-anxiety is not a better spreadsheet, because the wound was never a planning failure. It was a trust failure, a forgetting of whose child you are. And the gospel that reaches it is that the Father who feeds the birds did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, and the logic Paul draws is the only thing that ever quiets the three-in-the-morning math, that the God who gave you the greater thing at the cross will not abandon you over the lesser. He has already proven, at the highest possible cost, that He knows you are here.

scriptureStudy.note: Therefore do not be anxious about your life. The therefore links worry directly to the love of money in the verse before. Anxiety about provision is not a separate problem but the same idol felt from the underside, fear instead of hunger.

Look at the birds, your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value. The birds work but do not store against tomorrow as their security. The argument is from the lesser to the greater, from sparrows to sons.

Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life. Worry is exposed as not only faithless but useless, a tax on the soul that never buys the security it promises, draining the strength meant for the day at hand.

Consider the lilies, they neither toil nor spin, yet Solomon was not arrayed like one of these. The God who clothes a flower that lasts a day in glory beyond a king is not indifferent to the child He calls His own.

If God so clothes the grass, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith. Jesus names the real disorder, not a budget shortfall but little faith, a failure of trust that no amount of planning can heal.
Your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. The cure for anxiety is relational, not financial. He answers fear not with a plan but with a Father who already knows the need before it is spoken.

Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you. The verdict reorders the anxious life. Put the provision first and it eats you, put the kingdom first and the provision falls into place behind it, added not chased.

Do not be anxious about anything, but by prayer and thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. The antidote to worry is not silence but petition, handing the fear to a Father and receiving a peace that guards the heart.

memoryVerse.text: But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

sessions.title: The Freedom of the Open Hand
sessions.aim: To see generosity not as a duty laid on the reluctant but as the freedom of a heart that has stopped needing to hold, and to find under the cheerful giver the God who gave first.
sessions.summary: Paul tells the Corinthians that God loves a cheerful giver, and the word cheerful is the surprise, because we expect duty and he names joy. The session walks through the strange economy of generosity, the Macedonians who begged for the privilege of giving out of their poverty, the sowing that reaps in proportion, the giving that does not impoverish but frees. It takes the reader who hears all this as a fundraising pitch dressed in theology, the suspicion that talk of giving is always really talk of getting your money, and answers from the text. Paul is not after their money. He is after the grip the money has on them, because the open hand is not first a gift to the poor but a freedom for the giver, the hand that can release having proven it is no longer owned. Then the verdict that grounds the whole thing. You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. We give because we were given to first, at infinite cost. Bell stands inside it, a man whose fist has had to be pried open finger by finger. The session is the destination of the whole study, the heart finally free, the hand finally open, the treasure finally in the only place it cannot be lost.

keyScripture.why: Paul says God loves a cheerful giver, naming joy and not duty as the mark of true generosity, and revealing giving as the freedom of a heart no longer owned by what it holds.

discussion.q: Paul says God loves a cheerful giver, not a dutiful or a guilted one. Why does the cheerfulness matter so much to God, and what does reluctant giving reveal that the gift itself conceals?
discussion.behind: Open on the surprise of the word cheerful. We assume God mostly cares that the gift happens, but Paul says he cares how, that joy is the point and reluctance a symptom. The aim is to surface that giving with a clenched jaw reveals a heart that still believes the money is its security, while joyful giving reveals a heart that has been set free. Land the room on the diagnostic, not the duty.

discussion.q: The Macedonians, in deep poverty, begged for the privilege of giving, as though generosity were a gift being granted to them. How is that the opposite of how we usually feel about being asked to give?
discussion.behind: Get into the strangeness of the Macedonians, because they invert our instinct entirely. We feel asked-of, depleted, defensive. They felt let in on something, privileged. The point is that they had discovered generosity is not subtraction but freedom, and the poorer they were the more clearly they saw it. Help the room imagine wanting to give the way the Macedonians wanted to, and ask what they would have to believe to feel that.

discussion.q: Bell says the open hand is not first a gift to the poor but a freedom for the giver, the hand that can finally release having proven it is no longer owned. How does that change why a person gives and what giving does to him?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session and the study. Generosity is usually framed as something the giver does for the recipient. Bell reframes it as something that happens to the giver, the breaking of the grip, the proof that the leash from session one has been loosened. Help the room feel that the hand that can open is a hand that has been set free, and that the freedom is the deeper gift, the one given to the giver himself.

discussion.q: Bell takes seriously the suspicion that all church talk of giving is really talk of getting your money, a fundraising pitch in theological clothes. What is true in that suspicion, and how is Paul after something other than the Corinthians' cash?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness and disarm the cynic. The suspicion is earned, because giving has been manipulated in the church for centuries. But Paul refuses every manipulative lever, no compulsion, no shame, only the example of Christ. He is not after their money, he is after the grip the money has on them, the freedom on the far side of the open hand. Make sure the skeptic in the room feels his suspicion honored before it is gently answered.

discussion.q: Paul grounds all of it in Christ, who was rich and became poor so that we might become rich. Bell admits his own fist has had to be pried open finger by finger. Where is your fist still closed, and what would it take to believe you have already been given enough to open it?
discussion.behind: Close on the gospel and the self-implication, the destination of the whole study. We do not generate generosity, we receive it from the One who gave first at infinite cost. Bell does not pretend his hand opened easily, it had to be pried, finger by finger. Invite people to name the specific thing their fist is still closed around, and to hear that the open hand is possible only because Christ opened His first. Go first. Name your own pried-open finger.

objections.objection: This is just a fundraising pitch with a Bible verse on it. Every time the church talks about giving, what it really wants is my money, and dressing it up as freedom and joy does not change what it is.
objections.response: Honor the suspicion, because it is earned, the church has used guilt and manipulation to extract money for a very long time, and the cynicism is the scar of real abuse. But watch what Paul refuses to do. He will not compel, he says each one should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion. He uses no shame, no pressure, no quota. The only lever he pulls is the example of Christ. That is not how a fundraiser talks. Paul is not after the Corinthians' money, he is after the grip their money has on them, because he can see the giving is for the giver before it is ever for the poor, and a man who cannot open his hand is a man who is owned.

objections.objection: It is fine for the wealthy to talk about generous giving, but a person who barely has enough cannot afford to give it away. Generosity is a luxury for people whose own needs are already met.
objections.response: Grant the realism, because the study must never shame the person in genuine want or demand he give what he does not have. But notice who Paul holds up as the model. Not the wealthy. The Macedonians, in a severe test of affliction and their extreme poverty, overflowed in a wealth of generosity and begged for the privilege. The freedom of the open hand is not a luxury of the rich, it is most visible in the poor, because they have the least to hide behind and so the grip, when it breaks, breaks most plainly. This is not a command to the empty-handed to harm themselves. It is the testimony that the joy of the open hand has been found most often by those the world would say could least afford it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the one thing your hand is still closed around, and is it that you are holding it, or that it is holding you?
sessions.practice: This week, give one gift that costs you enough to feel it, quietly and cheerfully, expecting nothing back and telling no one. Afterward, pay attention not to what it did for the recipient but to what it did to you, and write down whether your hand felt poorer or freer.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, You were rich beyond measure and became poor to the point of a borrowed grave, so that we, who had nothing, could be made rich in the only wealth that lasts. We have held our money with a closed fist and called the closing security, and the holding has held us. Pry our fingers open, gently, the way You have always done it. Make us cheerful givers, not because we are commanded but because we are free, our treasure finally laid up with You where it cannot be lost, our hearts finally come home to where the treasure already is. To You who gave first, and gave everything, we open our hands. Amen.
reflection: Is my giving cheerful or reluctant, and what does the difference reveal about whether I own my money or it owns me?
If the open hand is first a freedom for the giver, what would releasing my grip actually set me free from?
Where is my fist still closed, and do I believe I have already been given enough, in Christ, to open it without fear?
sessions.teaching:
Paul is organizing a collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and everything about how he does it should surprise us, because it is the opposite of how money usually gets asked for. He will not compel. He will not shame. He will not set a quota or work the guilt. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. There is the word that breaks the expected mold. Cheerful. We assume God mostly wants the gift to happen and is not particular about the mood, that a reluctant gift still counts. Paul says no, that God loves the cheerful giver specifically, because the cheerfulness is the whole point. A reluctant gift reveals a heart that still believes the money is its security and is parting with a piece of its safety. A cheerful gift reveals a heart that has discovered the money was never its safety at all, and so can let it go laughing.

Then Paul holds up the strangest example he could have chosen. Not the wealthy, who could give without feeling it. The Macedonians, in a severe test of affliction and extreme poverty, who overflowed in a wealth of generosity, and who begged him, begged, for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints. Read that slowly, because it inverts everything we feel when an offering is mentioned. We feel asked-of, depleted, a little defensive, our hand instinctively closing. The Macedonians felt let in, privileged, as though generosity were a gift being granted to them rather than extracted from them. They had found something the comfortable rarely find, that giving is not subtraction. And they found it in poverty, which is no accident, because the poorer they were the less they had to hide behind, and the grip, when it finally broke, broke in plain sight.

Take the reader who hears all of this as a pitch, who has sat through enough manipulative offering talks to assume that any church conversation about giving is really a conversation about getting his money. Take him seriously, because the suspicion is earned. The church has used guilt and fear and false promises to pry money out of frightened people for a very long time, and his cynicism is the scar of real abuse. But watch what Paul refuses to do, and the refusal is the answer. He pulls none of the levers a fundraiser pulls. No compulsion, no shame, no quota, no veiled threat about what God will withhold. The only thing he holds up is the example of Christ. That is not a man working an angle. Paul is not after the Corinthians' money. He is after the grip the money has on them, because he understands the thing this whole study has been circling, that the open hand is first a freedom for the giver, and only second a gift to the poor.

And I have to be honest about my own hand, because it has never opened easily. It has had to be pried open, finger by finger, over years, by a God patient enough to do it slowly. I have given reluctantly and called it stewardship. I have calculated the gift down to what I could spare without feeling it and called the calculation wisdom. The truth is that my fist was closed because I was afraid, because the money felt like the wall between my five sons and the dark, and to open my hand felt like lowering the wall. What I could not see, for a long time, is that the wall was also a cage, that the hand closed around my security was a hand I no longer owned, and that the prying open, which felt like loss every single time, was God setting me free.

Then the verdict that grounds the whole thing and turns the duty into joy. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. There is why the giver can be cheerful, and there is the destination of everything this study has tried to say. We do not give in order to get. We do not give to earn. We give because we were given to first, at the highest imaginable cost, by a God who was rich beyond measure and emptied Himself to a borrowed grave so that we, who had nothing, could be made rich forever. The cheerful giver is simply a person who has finally believed that, whose treasure is now laid up where the moth cannot reach it, whose heart has followed the treasure home, who is no longer anxious because his Father has already proven everything at the cross, and whose hand, at long last, can open, because it has discovered it was holding nothing it could keep and being held by Someone it could never lose. That is the freedom. The open hand is not the cost of following Christ. It is the proof that you finally have.

scriptureStudy.note: In a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and extreme poverty overflowed in a wealth of generosity. The model is not the rich but the poor, in whom the broken grip is most visible, because they have the least to hide behind.

They gave of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part. They asked to give. Generosity was a privilege granted, not a burden imposed, the exact inverse of how we feel when an offering is named.

Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. The whole logic of giving rests here. We give because we were given to first, at infinite cost, by a God who emptied Himself.

Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. The image is sowing, not spending. The open hand is not loss but planting, releasing what could never be kept by holding it.

Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. The mood is the point. Reluctance reveals a heart still owned, cheerfulness a heart set free.

God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that you may abound in every good work. The supply for generosity is God's grace, not the giver's surplus, which is why the poor can give and the giver is never finally depleted.

You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way. The enrichment is for the purpose of generosity, not accumulation. What flows in is meant to flow out, the open hand both receiving and releasing.

It is more blessed to give than to receive. The freedom of the open hand is named by Jesus Himself, that the giver is the one who gains, because the gift that breaks the grip is the gift to the giver first.

memoryVerse.text: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

leaderPrimer: You did not have to do this, and the fact that you said yes matters more than you know. So before you open the first session, sit with me for a while, because this study will only go as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the material. It is settling your own heart. The aim of this series is narrow and it is hard. It is to follow the heart to its treasure, to face what money has quietly done to us, and to arrive, by the end, at the freedom of an open hand under the One who became poor so we could be rich. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to make anyone feel guilty for having. It is not to produce a room of people ashamed of their savings or their homes or their wish to provide for the people they love. If anyone leaves this series clutching his money tighter, only now with a layer of shame on top of the clutching, the study failed, because the goal was never guilt. Guilt changes nothing and curdles into resentment. The goal is freedom, the loosened grip, the heart finally come home to its treasure. Keep that in front of you, because the single greatest danger you face as a leader is the temptation to turn this study into a lever for behavior you want to see, and that temptation will not feel like manipulation. It will feel like passion, like finally getting people to be generous, like righteous urgency about their souls. Refuse it. The moment the room senses you are trying to get something out of them, their money or their guilt or their agreement, the hands close, and a study about the open hand has produced the opposite of its aim. Here is the most important distinction you will guard the whole way through, and you must hold it cleanly. There is a difference between having money and being owned by it. The Bible does not condemn the first and will not let us excuse the second. Jesus does not tell most people he meets to get rid of their possessions, he tells everyone to watch where their treasure is laid up, because the heart goes there. A person in your group may have a great deal and hold it with an open hand, and a person beside him may have almost nothing and worship the little he has or the more he lacks. The line does not run between the rich and the poor in the room. It runs through every heart present, including yours. Say this out loud early and often. We are not here to decide who has too much. We are here to ask what our money has done to our hearts, and that question reaches the man with the full barn and the man with the empty one alike. Now keep the room safe, because depth requires safety and money is one of the least safe topics there is. People carry shame about debt, fear about scarcity, guilt about having, grief about losing, resentment about not having, and any of it can detonate. Safety here does not mean comfort. It means a person can be honest out loud without being humiliated, can confess a fear about money without it being used against him, can admit his hand is closed without being made the villain of the evening. Never shame debt. The man drowning in it did not necessarily sin his way there, and the study must never let the room imply he did, because a medical bill and a layoff are not moral failures, and Jesus never treated poverty as a verdict. Never shame having, either. The comfortable person in your room is not the enemy, he is a fellow patient, and if you turn him into the cautionary tale the others will quietly decide the study is about someone other than themselves, which is the death of it. And never, ever promise prosperity. This is not a study that tells anyone faith will fatten his account. If it drifts that direction you have lost the whole thing, because Paul said plainly that the desire to be rich is the trap, and the prosperity gospel is simply the love of money with a worship song. Set these expectations in the first session and guard them every session after. The facilitator script gives you words. Use them. You will face three rooms, and you should know them before they arrive. The first is the defended person, the one who came braced, certain this study is going to guilt him about his money or pry into his accounts. Do not match his guard with pressure. Find the half of his defensiveness that is true, because there usually is one. The man who suspects church money-talk is really after his wallet is right that it often has been. Grant that fully and mean it, and tell him this study refuses every lever, no guilt, no quota, no shame, and watch his shoulders come down. The second is the hurt person, the one who is in debt, or was, or is genuinely poor, and who hears every sentence about money through the memory of an empty account and a sleepless night. Do not let the discussion treat scarcity as a thought experiment in front of someone who has lived it. Honor the person, slow down, and make sure the room knows the study never blames anyone for what he lacks and never tells the anxious to simply stop being afraid. The third is the silent room, the one where nobody will go first because money is the thing nobody talks about honestly, where people will discuss their marriages before they will discuss their bank balances. The cure is not a better question. It is your own confession. Go first, name your own grip and your own three-in-the-morning arithmetic and your own pried-open fist, and the room will slowly follow you into the honesty you modeled. Silence after a hard question about money is almost always people doing painful math in their heads. Count to ten before you rescue it. Now the part that matters most, the part it would be easiest to skip. Your own heart. You cannot lead people somewhere you have not gone. If you walk in as the man who already holds money rightly, the free one helping the captives, you have already failed, because Bell does not stand there and neither can you. He has lain awake doing arithmetic he called prudence. He has felt his chest loosen at a number and called the loosening peace. He has loved his five sons and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough. He has given reluctantly and called it stewardship, and watched his own fist have to be pried open finger by finger over years. He writes from inside the indictment about money, and the power of the whole series depends on you doing the same. So before session one, sit with this yourself. Find the place where your grip runs out of order. Name the security you would be slowest to release. Locate the worry you have dressed as responsibility, the giving you have used to close a question, the number that has lied to you about your soul. If you cannot find any of this in yourself, you are not ready to lead, because either you serve God and money both with a clean and undivided heart, which the gospel says you do not, or you cannot yet see your own divided one, which means you will lead from above the room instead of inside it. The leader whose own hand is being pried open can call others to freedom without contempt. The leader who imagines his is already open will turn the study into a guilt trip, which is the same closed fist pointed at someone else's wallet. One more practical word before the charge. Watch the clock and the temperature together. These sessions will run long if you let every objection become a debate, so you are not aiming to win each point but to hold the room in the honest tension and then pray. When a conversation gets tender, and it will, because money is tender, slow your own voice rather than pressing, name what is true in what was just said, and move the table toward the practice and the reflection, because none of this lands as an idea argued. It lands as a thing carried out into the week. Trust the closing prayer to do work the discussion cannot. End every session there, even when nothing felt resolved, because Bell does not resolve these essays either, and a room sent out carrying weight will come back changed in a way a room sent out satisfied never will. Resist the urge to tie a bow. The unresolved ending is not a failure of the study. It is the design. Here is your charge. You are not the judge of this room, and you are certainly not its accountant. You are a fellow patient who happens to be holding the readings, a man whose own fist is still being pried open, leading others toward a freedom you are also only beginning to taste. Lead like one. Let the weight of these sessions rest on you first and hardest. Refuse every chance to make this about someone else's money or someone else's greed or the people who are not present. Keep the cross above the ledger in your own heart before you ask anyone else to, and when you fail at it, say so out loud, because your failure honestly named will teach the room more than your competence ever could. The goal is not a room that gives more by the end, though it may. The goal is a room full of people, you first, who can hold money with an open hand, whose hearts have followed their treasure to the only place it cannot be lost, and who can no longer remember why they ever thought a fuller barn would feed the soul. Go gently. Go honestly. Go first.

faq.q: Is this study just a way to make people feel guilty about money or pressure them to give more?
faq.a: No, and the study works hard to prove it. The aim is not guilt, which changes nothing and curdles into resentment, but freedom, the loosened grip and the open hand. The fifth session is emphatic that Paul refuses every manipulative lever, no compulsion, no shame, no quota, only the example of Christ, because God loves a cheerful giver and a gift squeezed out by guilt is not the thing he is after. The study never shames the person who has and never demands that anyone give what he does not have. The target is never having money. It is what the heart has quietly done with money, the grip that has come to grip back. If you came braced for an attack on your wallet, you will find instead a question about your heart, and it is aimed at the writer and the leader first.

faq.q: Is the Bible against having money or wanting to provide for my family?
faq.a: No, and the study is careful here. Jesus does not tell most people he meets to get rid of their possessions, and he says lay up treasure, only somewhere the moth and rust and thief cannot reach it. Provision is honored in Scripture, the ant who stores in summer is praised, and the wish to care for those you love is good. What Jesus warns against is the location and the leash, laying up treasure where it will rot and take your heart down with it, and letting the love of money, the craving, become the master of a heart that can serve only one. So having is not the sin. Being owned by what you have is. The question is never whether you may have money, but whether your money has quietly come to have you.

faq.q: What is the difference between this study and the Economic Justice study?
faq.a: They are companions, not duplicates, and they look in opposite directions on purpose. The Economic Justice study looks outward, at systems, at whether poverty is political, at the Jubilee economy, at the difference between charity and justice, at the structures money lives inside. This study looks inward, at the heart, at what money does to the soul of the person holding it, at greed and contentment and anxiety and the open hand. One asks what we owe the poor man at the gate. This one asks what our treasure has done to our own hearts before God. You can run them in either order, but do not expect this study to cover systemic questions, because it stays deliberately on the individual heart, where Jesus aimed most of what he said about money.

faq.q: Does the Bible actually say money is evil?
faq.a: No, and the study is careful here. Paul does not say money is the root of evil. He says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils, one root among others, and the word he uses describes a craving, a reaching, a stretch toward. The danger is the wanting, not the coin, and the wanting can live in a poor man as easily as a rich one. Money itself is a created good. The deeper claim the study makes is that money is not neutral either, that Jesus personifies it as mammon, a rival lord, and says you cannot serve God and money. So money is real, good, and dangerous, all at once. The error is to treat it as morally blank, a tool you are safely in charge of, when Scripture treats it as a power that wants your heart.

faq.q: Is contentment just a religious way of telling people to settle for less than they deserve?
faq.a: It can be misused that way, preached at struggling people to keep them quiet, and the study names that abuse honestly. But that is not what Paul means, and the text proves it. Paul is the least passive person in the New Testament, working and striving and driving himself, and he writes about contentment not from comfort but from a prison cell and from hunger. His contentment is not the absence of effort but the absence of dependence, a freedom that lets him strive without being enslaved to the outcome. Contentment is not the death of desire either. It is desire finally aimed at the one thing built to satisfy it. The contented person is not the one who has stopped wanting better. He is the one whose peace no longer hangs on whether better arrives.

faq.q: Why does Jesus call the rich man in the parable a fool when he just worked hard and planned ahead?
faq.a: Because the folly is not the barn. The man breaks no commandment, and Scripture does commend saving and planning. Read his speech and you find what Jesus is naming. He says my crops, my barns, my goods, my soul, and in the whole monologue there is no God, no neighbor, no one but himself, and he tells his soul to eat and be merry, as though a soul were a stomach. He built a magnificent future for his body and forgot entirely that he had a soul, securing everything that could be taken from him and ignoring the one thing that could be lost forever. The parable does not forbid planning. It asks why we plan so carefully for the shorter life and leave the longer one to chance, and it does the kindness of reminding us we do not know the length of either.

faq.q: Is it cruel to tell an anxious or struggling person not to worry about money?
faq.a: It would be, if it were said the way we usually say it, and the study refuses that glib version. A do not worry tossed at a frightened person is a small cruelty the church has committed often. But look at how Jesus gives the command. He does not bark it and move on. He reasons, patiently, consider the birds, look at the lilies, your Father knows what you need, building a case for trust rather than demanding a feeling by willpower. He is not commanding the frightened child to stop feeling. He is giving the heart something true and solid to rest on so the fear has somewhere else to go. And he says it as one who knew hunger and would die with nothing, not from a comfortable distance. The study treats money-anxiety as a wound to be healed, not a flaw to be scolded.

faq.q: I do not really struggle with money or think about it much. Is this study even for me?
faq.a: Yes, and maybe more than you expect. The two masters do not fight loudly in the heart that has quietly made peace with one of them. Jesus warns the person who does not chase wealth as much as the one who does, because the heart can serve money through fear of not having it as surely as through hunger to get more, and the anxious frugal person and the ambitious reaching person may be bowing to the same master in different postures. The study asks you to look not only at your wanting but at your worry, not only at your spending but at where your mind goes at three in the morning. Simplicity is a real good, but do not assume that because you are not greedy you are free. The question reaches the comfortable and the cautious as surely as the grasping.

faq.q: Is giving really for the poor, or is this just another church asking for money?
faq.a: The suspicion is earned, because the church has used guilt and false promises to pry money out of frightened people for a long time, and the study honors the cynicism rather than scolding it. But Paul, gathering a collection, pulls none of the levers a fundraiser pulls, no compulsion, no shame, no quota, only the example of Christ. He is not after the Corinthians' money. He is after the grip the money has on them, because he understands that the open hand is first a freedom for the giver and only second a gift to the poor. A man who cannot open his hand is a man who is owned. The study cares about giving not to fill a plate but because the hand that can finally release has proven it is no longer held by what it was holding.

faq.q: Does refusing the prosperity gospel mean God does not want to bless me?
faq.a: No. The study affirms that God is a Father who gives good gifts, that creation is good, and that Scripture is full of feasting and provision. God does bless, often with abundance. What the study refuses is the move that bolts a craving onto the blessing and baptizes the reaching, that tells you the stretch toward more is faith when Paul says plainly the desire to be rich is the trap. The prosperity gospel is simply the love of money with a worship song over it. You can receive blessing as a gift with gratitude and still refuse to let the wanting become your master. The error is never the gift. It is the craving fastened to it, and the trust quietly transferred from the Giver to the thing given.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the writer and the leader instead of pointing at greedy people?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is the message. Bell does not stand outside this. He has lain awake doing arithmetic he called prudence, felt his chest loosen at a number and called it peace, given reluctantly and called it stewardship, watched his own fist have to be pried open finger by finger. He writes from inside the indictment, not from a safe distance, and the study asks every leader to do the same. The reason is not false modesty. It is that you cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue, and you cannot call others to freedom from a height without turning the call into contempt or a guilt trip. A study that pointed only at the absent greedy would let everyone present off the hook. By keeping the writer and the leader inside it, the study makes the open hand possible for the people actually in the room.

faq.q: What if I am in debt and money already keeps me up at night? Will this study just make it worse?
faq.a: It should not, if it is led the way it was written, because the study refuses to treat debt as a moral failure or to scold the anxious for being afraid. A medical bill, a layoff, a hard season, these are not sins, and the leader is told plainly never to let the room imply otherwise. What the study offers the worried heart is not a harder push but a Father, the One who feeds the birds and clothes the grass and knows what you need before you ask, because the wound of money-anxiety is finally a wound of trust, and trust is healed by a Person, not a spreadsheet. If you carry fear about money to bed, this study means to meet you there with something truer to rest on, not to add shame to the load you are already carrying.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have no training and money makes me anxious too?
faq.a: You lead it the way it was built to be led, by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than argument, and the teaching notes, scripture studies, and leader primer mean you are never improvising. But the real qualification is not training, and it is certainly not having your own finances figured out. It is willingness to go first, to be honest about your own grip and your own reaching, to keep the room safe for people who carry shame about debt or fear about scarcity, and to refuse to turn the study into a guilt trip. Your anxiety about money is not a disqualification. It is your way in, the thing that lets you stand inside the indictment with everyone else rather than above the room. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart, and trust the material.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here. Before we start, three things. First, this study is not about anyone's bank account but about everyone's heart, including mine, so we are not here to decide who has too much or to pry into anyone's accounts. Second, nobody has to perform. You can be honest about a fear or a grip without it being used against you, and you can change your mind out loud. Third, the writer puts himself inside everything he says, and so will we. He has lain awake doing arithmetic he called prudence, felt his chest loosen at a number and called it peace, watched his own fist have to be pried open. We are not pointing from a safe distance. We are standing in it. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the passage says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the week we are about to walk into, because none of this matters if it stays an idea about other people's money or other people's hearts.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because Bell does not resolve it either and neither should we. Take the weight of this out with you rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go, and then I will see you next time. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation about the thing none of us usually talk about.

plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set ground rules, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Where Your Treasure Is, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, The Secret of Contentment, with extended time on contentment as a learned freedom.

Week 6: Session 4 continued, seek first the kingdom and the Father who knows, plus practice.

bibliography.title: Counterfeit Gods: The Empty Promises of Money, Sex, and Power
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Where Keller shows how money becomes an idol that hides inside virtue and presents itself as security and prudence. Anchors sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Treasure Principle
bibliography.author: Randy Alcorn
bibliography.note: A short, pointed treatment of laying up treasure in heaven and the freedom of giving, useful background for sessions 1 and 5. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to the study.

bibliography.title: Money, Possessions, and Eternity
bibliography.author: Randy Alcorn
bibliography.note: A fuller survey of the Bible's teaching on wealth, contentment, and generosity that refuses both the prosperity pole and the poverty pole. Background across all five sessions, leader to confirm before pressing specifics.

bibliography.title: Neither Poverty Nor Riches: A Biblical Theology of Possessions
bibliography.author: Craig Blomberg
bibliography.note: A careful survey holding together the Bible's affirmation of material goods and its severe warnings about wealth, refusing both poles. Useful as a balancing voice across the study.

bibliography.title: The Ruthless Elimination of Hurry
bibliography.author: John Mark Comer
bibliography.note: Names the anxious, acquisitive restlessness of the modern heart and the contentment found in another kind of life. A pastoral companion for sessions 2 and 4. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them.

bibliography.title: Money and Power
bibliography.author: Jacques Ellul
bibliography.note: Argues money is not a tool we picked up but a power we serve, and the pretense that it is neutral is the lie that lets it rule the heart. Anchors session 1.

bibliography.title: The Freedom of Simplicity
bibliography.author: Richard J. Foster
bibliography.note: On the inward and outward freedom of holding possessions with an open hand, neither despising them nor being mastered by them. Supports sessions 2 and 5. Leader to confirm specifics.

bibliography.title: Sin: A History
bibliography.author: Gary A. Anderson
bibliography.note: Shows how sin came to be pictured as a debt and forgiveness as its release, illuminating why the language of treasure and debt runs so deep in Scripture. Background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: On Wealth and Poverty
bibliography.author: John Chrysostom
bibliography.note: The fourth-century homilies that refuse to let the comfortable hide from the words of Jesus about wealth and the soul. Cited in sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: On the single-hearted following that cannot serve two masters and the call that will not be reduced to comfortable terms. Supports the verdict of session 1. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them.

glossary.definition: The Aramaic word Jesus personifies as a rival lord, a god with a small g that asks not for worship in words but for your trust, a little more each year. Not money as such, but money treated as a master.

Whatever the heart stores and follows. Jesus says where the treasure is the heart will be also, making your treasure the truest map of your loves, and warning that treasure laid up on earth rots and takes the heart with it.

Not the death of desire or resignation to less, but a learned freedom, desire finally aimed at the one thing that satisfies it, so that neither plenty nor want can move the heart off its center. Paul calls it a secret, learned in a prison.

The grasping inward reach for what is not yours, the greedy eye Jesus says darkens the whole body. It rarely announces itself, hiding inside ordinary planning and the language of fairness, which is why Jesus says be on your guard against it.

Jesus' image in Matthew 6:22-23, literally the bad eye, an idiom for a grasping, calculating gaze. What the eye fixes on fills the whole body with light or dark, so a heart always doing arithmetic on its gain is darkening all the way through.

The wealth the rich fool lacked, treasure stored in God rather than in barns, the only account the night cannot require away. It is the alternative the parable holds out so that the warning is not mere terror but an invitation.

The image of a heart no longer owned by what it holds, able to release without fear because its security rests elsewhere. The open hand is first a freedom for the giver and only second a gift to the poor.

Paul's phrase in 2 Corinthians 9:7. The mood is the diagnosis. A reluctant gift reveals a heart still trusting its money for security, a cheerful gift a heart set free, which is why God loves the cheerful one specifically.

The view that faith claims material abundance and that godliness is a means of gain. Right that creation is good and God blesses, but it bolts a craving onto blessing and baptizes the reaching Paul calls the trap, the love of money with a worship song over it.

The theological idea that God gives genuine gifts, order, beauty, provision, to all people, which lets Christians receive material blessing with gratitude and honor real good without worshiping wealth or despising the body and the field.

The holding of money and possessions as a trust from God rather than an absolute possession, with an open hand and an account to give. A true word that we have sometimes used as a costume over a closed fist, calling reluctance prudence.

Bell's image from session 1 for the way the heart follows the treasure rather than leading it, going where the money and the worry have already gone. To find what you love, follow the leash from your heart to where it has been pulled.

Contentment is not the death of desire. It is desire finally aimed at the one thing that can satisfy it.
He secured everything that could be taken from him and forgot the one thing that could be lost forever.
Worry is the love of money felt from the underside, the worship of money wearing the face of fear.
The cure for money-anxiety was never a better spreadsheet. The wound was a trust failure, and only a Father reaches it.
The open hand is not first a gift to the poor. It is a freedom for the giver, the proof that he is no longer owned.
A reluctant gift reveals a heart still owned. A cheerful one reveals a heart set free.
He was rich, and became poor, so that we who had nothing could be made rich forever. So open your hand.
